title: The business case technique: develop, check, maintain, confirm
blurb: Describe the four steps of the business case technique and the three basic business options, with 'do nothing differently' as the baseline.
question: A project manager assesses a newly raised risk to see whether the project is still justified. Which step of the business case technique is this?

teach.h: Four steps for managing the business case
teach.body: Formally: the PRINCE2 technique for the business case has four steps: develop, check, maintain and confirm. Develop builds the outline and then the full business case; check assesses whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable; maintain updates it with progress and forecasts; confirm assesses whether the intended benefits have been, or will be, realized. In plain English: write it, test it, keep it current, prove it paid off.

teach.caption: Develop, check and maintain happen inside the project; confirm continues after it.

teach.body: The project mandate triggers starting up a project and is used to develop the outline business case. In initiation it is refined into the full business case, which the project board approves when authorizing the project. Developing it involves analysing options and an investment appraisal, which compares the costs of developing, operating and maintaining the products with the value of the benefits over a period of time.

teach.caption: The difference between the options is the benefit that the investment will buy.

teach.body: Do nothing differently is the first option considered and the basis for quantifying the others: it shows what happens if the project does not go ahead. The extra benefit of doing the minimum, or more than the minimum, is measured against it. Even a compulsory project compares options, because it must justify the option chosen to comply as the best overall value.

teach.h: Check: who checks it, and when
head: Who
When the business case is checked
rows: End of each stage; assessing an exception plan
At project end; when stakeholder objectives change
teach.caption: Each check asks whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable, refining the case as costs, timescales, products and risks become clearer.

teach.body: Maintain: at the end of each stage the project manager updates the business case with progress data, such as products delivered, costs and benefits realized, plus the latest forecasts of benefits and performance targets. Confirm: assess whether the intended benefits have been, or will be, realized. Most confirmation happens after closure in post-project benefits reviews by the business, though some benefits are realized during the project when products are released iteratively.

steps.label: Maintain
steps.sub: PM updates with data and forecasts

teach.body: Brackenfield Foods' packaging line is ageing. Project manager Tom Adeyemi develops the outline business case with three options: keep the current line (do nothing differently), refurbish it (do the minimum) or buy a new automated line (do more than the minimum). Measured against the first option, refurbishment saves £60,000 a year and a new line £150,000. The full business case backs the new line. At each stage end Tom maintains it with actual spend; after go-live the business confirms the savings.

teach.text: Classic trap: confusing check with maintain. Maintain is updating the business case with progress data and forecasts at a stage end; check is judging whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable. Second trap: 'do nothing differently' is not a rejected option to drop; it is the baseline every other option is measured against.

items: Four steps: develop, check, maintain, confirm.
Develop: mandate to outline (starting up) to full (initiation); board approves when authorizing the project.
Three options: do nothing differently (first, the baseline), do the minimum, do more than the minimum.
Check: board at decision points and exception plans; PM when assessing progress, risks and issues.
Maintain: PM updates at each stage end. Confirm: benefits realized, mostly after closure.

summary: You can now describe the develop, check, maintain and confirm steps and say who performs each and when. You can also explain the three basic business options and why 'do nothing differently' is the baseline for valuing the others.

A.q: What are the four steps of the PRINCE2 business case technique?
A.why: The PRINCE2 7 business case technique steps are develop, check, maintain and confirm (manual 5.3.1).

whyNot.0: The PRINCE2 7 steps are check and maintain, not verify and approve.
whyNot.2: 'Identify' and 'assess' belong to the risk technique.
whyNot.3: Approve, monitor and close are not the named steps of the technique.

A.q: Which business option should be considered first and used as the basis for quantifying the other options?
A.why: Do nothing differently is the first option and the basis for quantifying the others; the difference between the options is the benefit the investment buys.

whyNot.0: Doing the minimum is valued against the baseline; it is not the baseline itself.
whyNot.1: This fuller option is also measured against the baseline.
whyNot.2: The preferred option is chosen after the options have been compared with the baseline.

A.q: In which step of the business case technique does the project manager update the business case with progress data and the latest forecasts at the end of each stage?
A.why: Maintain: at each stage end the project manager updates the business case with progress data and latest forecasts (manual 5.3.1.3).

whyNot.0: Confirm assesses whether benefits have been or will be realized.
whyNot.1: Develop produces the outline and full business case.
whyNot.3: Check judges whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable.

B.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. During the [?] step, the business case is assessed to judge whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable.
B.why: The check step assesses whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable.

whyNot.1: Maintain updates the business case with progress data and forecasts.
whyNot.2: Confirm assesses whether benefits have been or will be realized.
whyNot.3: Develop creates the outline and full business case.

B.q: A project manager assesses a newly raised risk to understand its effect on the project's business justification. Which step of the business case technique is being applied?
B.why: The project manager checks the business case when assessing progress, risks and issues, to judge their impact on business justification (manual 5.3.1.2).

whyNot.0: Develop is building the outline and full business case.
whyNot.2: Maintain is the stage-end update with progress data and forecasts.
whyNot.3: Confirm assesses whether benefits are realized, mostly after closure.

B.q:
Which two statements about the business case technique are correct?
1. The difference between the business options is the benefit the investment will buy.
2. Confirming benefits mostly takes place before the project closes.
3. An investment appraisal compares the costs of developing, operating and maintaining the products with the value of the benefits over a period.
4. Compulsory projects do not need to justify the option chosen.
B.why: The difference between the options is the benefit the investment buys (1), and the investment appraisal compares lifetime costs with the value of benefits over time (3).

whyNot.1: Statement 4 is false: compulsory projects still justify the option chosen.
whyNot.2: Statement 2 is false: confirming benefits mostly happens after closure.
whyNot.3: Both are false: confirmation is mostly after closure, and compulsory projects justify the chosen option.

C.q: When does the project board check the business case during delivery, and which step updates it just before that check?
C.why: The board checks the business case at the end of each stage before authorizing the next; the project manager maintains it with actuals and forecasts first.

whyNot.0: Highlight reports are periodic progress reports, not the decision point for checking the business case.
whyNot.1: The decision point is right, but confirm assesses benefits realized, mostly after closure.
whyNot.3: Highlight reports are not the decision point, and develop belongs to starting up and initiation.

C.q: A food manufacturer compares keeping its current line, refurbishing it, or buying a new automated line. Which statement is correct?
options: Refurbishing is the baseline for valuing the others
Keeping the current line is dropped as it brings no change
Buying the new line is the baseline as it is preferred
Keeping the current line is the baseline for the others
C.why: Keeping the current line is 'do nothing differently': the first option and the basis for quantifying the other two.

whyNot.0: Refurbishing is 'do the minimum', which is valued against the baseline.
whyNot.1: The baseline is not dropped: it is what every other option is measured against.
whyNot.2: The preferred option is chosen by comparison with the baseline; it is not the baseline.

C.q: Which statement about the confirm step is correct?
options: It approves the full business case before delivery stages
It assesses whether intended benefits have been realized
It updates the business case with actual costs each stage
It judges whether the project remains desirable and viable
C.why: Confirm assesses whether the intended benefits have been (or will be) realized, mostly after closure (manual 5.3.1.4).

whyNot.0: Approving the full business case happens when the board authorizes the project.
whyNot.2: Updating with actual costs at each stage end is the maintain step.
whyNot.3: Judging continued desirability and viability is the check step.

reteach.title: Choosing a new boiler
reteach.question: Your boiler is old. How would you decide whether to keep it, repair it or replace it, and how would you know later that you chose well?

blocks.body: First you ask what happens if you change nothing: rising bills and the odd breakdown. That is your baseline. Then you price a repair (do the minimum) and a new boiler (do more than the minimum), and compare each with the baseline. You write up your choice (develop), test it when new quotes arrive (check), update it as the work goes on (maintain) and look at your bills a year later (confirm).

blocks.text: Maintain updates the case with facts and forecasts; check judges whether it is still worth it. They often happen together at a stage end, but they are different steps.

explain.body: The project mandate triggers starting up and is used to develop the outline business case, refined into the full business case in initiation.

test.q: What triggers starting up a project and provides the input for developing the outline business case?
test.why: The project mandate activates starting up a project and is used to develop the outline business case (manual 5.3.1.1).

whyNot.1: The project brief is assembled in starting up and contains the outline business case.
whyNot.2: The initiation notice comes after the board authorizes initiation.
whyNot.3: The project plan is prepared later, in initiation.

explain.body: Do nothing differently (the baseline), do the minimum, and do more than the minimum. The difference between them is the benefit the investment buys.

test.q: What does the difference between the three basic business options represent?
options: The risk budget for the project
The change budget for each stage
test.why: The difference between do nothing differently, do the minimum and do more than the minimum is the benefit that the investment will buy.

whyNot.0: A risk budget funds risk responses.
whyNot.1: Cost tolerance is the permitted deviation in cost.
whyNot.3: A change budget funds approved changes.

explain.body: The board checks at the end of starting up, initiation and each stage, and when assessing an exception plan. The project manager checks when assessing progress, risks and issues.

test.q: At which point does the project board check the business case?
options: When a team manager accepts a work package
When a checkpoint report is received
When a product passes its quality review
test.why: The board checks the business case at each decision point and when assessing an exception plan.

whyNot.0: Accepting a work package is between the team manager and project manager.
whyNot.1: Checkpoint reports go from team manager to project manager.
whyNot.2: Quality reviews check products against their specifications.

explain.body: The business reviews the business case in post-project benefits reviews to see whether the intended benefits were realized.

test.q: Who reviews the business case in post-project benefits reviews?
test.why: After closure, the business reviews the business case in post-project benefits reviews (manual 5.3.1.4).

whyNot.0: The project manager's role ends at closure.
whyNot.2: Team managers deliver products during the project.
whyNot.3: Project support provides administrative help during the project.
